nodes.label: W1 · Sustainability & Environmental Ethics
nodes.summary: Week 1: definitions, history and dimensions of sustainability, ecosystems and ecological laws, and environmental ethics theories.
nodes.details:
Week 1 sets the conceptual foundation for the whole course (WI1103 Introduction to Sustainability Principles). It has two halves:

- **Part 1 – What is sustainability?** Sustainability as an *open-ended, temporary* concept; a **timeline** from Carlowitz (1713) to Brundtland's *Our Common Future*; the **three dimensions** (economic, environmental, social) and the **Doughnut Economics** model; the **environment and ecosystems** (biotic + abiotic, energy flow, nutrient cycling); how **human activities** alter ecosystems; and the **laws of ecology**.
- **Part 2 – Environmental ethics.** Opens with the farrowing-crate livestock case, then asks what ethics is, and walks through a spectrum of positions: the **Dominion thesis**, Locke, **anthropocentrism** and **utilitarianism**, **stewardship**, Pinchot's **conservationism** vs Muir's **preservationism** (the **Hetch Hetchy** dam dispute), and Aldo Leopold's **Land Ethic / ecocentrism**. It ends with a **dam-vs-salmon conservation dilemma**.

The ethics spectrum (human-centred → nature-centred) is a recurring lens for later weeks: valuing ecosystem services (W4), trade-offs between SDGs (W7) and who bears responsibility for planetary boundaries (W2).

nodes.label: Part 1 · What is sustainability?
nodes.summary: Definitions and history of sustainability, its three dimensions, Doughnut Economics, ecosystems, human impacts, and the laws of ecology.
nodes.details:
The lecture's first half answers six guiding questions (slide 9):

1. **What is the definition of sustainability?** – an open-ended, temporary, socially constructed concept (slide 11).
2. **When did sustainability start being discussed?** – timeline 1713 → 2003 (slide 12).
3. **What are its dimensions?** – economic, environmental, social, and their overlaps; extended by **Doughnut Economics** (slides 13–14).
4. **Environment and ecosystems** – the environment is *foundational*; ecosystems are biotic + abiotic units linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling (slides 15–16).
5. **Human impacts on ecosystems** – all activities alter energy flows and cycles, shifting the ecosystem functions society depends on (slide 17).
6. **Ecological law** – six laws of ecology, e.g. *everything must go somewhere*, *no free lunch* (slide 18).

The logic runs from *concept* (what we mean) → *structure* (dimensions, nested in the environment) → *science* (ecosystems and their laws) → *why it matters* (human disruption).

nodes.label: Sustainability is open-ended & temporary
nodes.summary: Sustainability cannot be fixed scientifically once and for all: it is an open-ended, positive, temporary concept shaped by time, situation, culture and knowledge.
nodes.details:
Slide 11 asks: **can sustainability be scientifically defined?** The answer given is no single fixed definition exists. Sustainability should be understood as an **open-ended, positive and temporary** concept:

- **Open-ended** – the *social understanding* of sustainable development depends on **time and situation, culture and knowledge**; it keeps evolving.
- **Positive** – it describes a desirable direction, not just the avoidance of harm.
- **Temporary** – any definition reflects its era and will be revised.

The slide's chart (Hopwood et al. 2005) **maps views of sustainable development** on two axes: *increasing environmental concern* (techno-centred → eco-centred) and *increasing socio-economic well-being & equality concern*. Positions range from **status quo** (e.g. World Bank, OECD, WBCSD, neo-liberal economists), through **reform** (e.g. Brundtland, ICLEI, IUCN), to **transformation** (e.g. social ecology, eco-socialism, indigenous/Global South movements, deep ecology).

Why it matters: the same word supports very different agendas – this is why the course keeps asking *whose* sustainability, and links to the ethics spectrum in Part 2 and to the SDG framing in W5.

**Quiz 1 phrasing:** sustainability is described as an **ethical concept** - a vision of *how the world ought to be* - rather than a scientifically derivable fact; it is open-ended, not static, not closed-ended and not a linear economic model.
nodes.examTips: Be ready to explain WHY sustainability can't be defined once scientifically (depends on time, situation, culture, knowledge). Hopwood's map: techno-centred vs eco-centred; status quo vs reform vs transformation. Quiz 1: sustainability is fundamentally an ETHICAL concept (a vision of "how the world should be"), not a static scientific fact, not a linear economic model, not a closed-ended universal definition.

nodes.label: Timeline of the sustainability idea
nodes.summary: From Carlowitz's sustainable forestry (1713) through Malthus, 1960s ecological economists, Brundtland, the German Advisory Council (1994) to multidimensional concepts (2003).
nodes.details:
Slide 12 traces the idea of sustainability:

- **1713 – Hans Carl von Carlowitz**, German mining director: called for "continuous, stable and sustainable utilization of forests" (timber for mining) – the origin of *Nachhaltigkeit*.
- **Thomas Malthus** (economist; slide dates it 1850, his famous essay was 1798): identified the imbalance between a habitat's resources and its population, predicting **famine, epidemics and war** – the first systematic study of **ecological limits to growth**.
- **1960s – Boulding, Ayres & Kneese, Georgescu-Roegen, Daly** (economists): after many environmental disasters made the environment a public concern, they put **nature back on the economic agenda** (roots of ecological economics).
- **1983 – Brundtland Commission (WCED)**: produced *Our Common Future* defining sustainable development; environment, economy and society are **interdependent** (see child node).
- **1994 – German Advisory Council**: three responsibilities – to the **natural environment**, to the **social world**, and to **itself**.
- **2003** – sustainability concepts divided into **unidimensional** and **multidimensional**.

The arc: from managing one resource (forests) → limits to growth → integrated multi-dimensional development.
nodes.examTips: Know the order and who did what: Carlowitz (forests) → Malthus (population vs resources) → 1960s economists → Brundtland/WCED → German Advisory Council's 3 responsibilities. Quiz 1: Malthus (dated ~1850 on the slide and in the quiz) = first systematic study of ecological limits to growth; not Carlowitz (forestry, 1713), Leopold, Muir or Pinchot.

nodes.label: Brundtland / Our Common Future
nodes.summary: WCED report Our Common Future: development meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs; environment, economy, society interdependent.
nodes.details:
The **World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED)**, chaired by Gro Harlem **Brundtland** (set up 1983; report published 1987), produced ***Our Common Future***, the classic source of the definition of **sustainable development**:

> development that **meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**.

Key points from the slides:
- The report explains that **environment, economy and society are interdependent and interconnected** – the basis of the three-dimension model (slide 13).
- The slide on dimensions reuses the same wording for the **economic dimension**, showing how central the Brundtland formula is.
- It embeds **intergenerational equity** (fairness to future generations) and, implicitly, intragenerational equity (meeting needs of all now).

It is the bridge between early resource-limit thinking (Carlowitz, Malthus) and the later **SDGs** (W5), which operationalise sustainable development into goals, targets and indicators.
nodes.examTips: Quote the Brundtland definition accurately. Note the slide dates the Commission to 1983 (founding); the report itself is 1987.

nodes.label: Three dimensions of sustainability
nodes.summary: Economic, environmental and social dimensions; their overlaps are bearable, equitable and viable, and all three together are sustainable.
nodes.details:
Slide 13 defines three **dimensions (pillars)**:

- **Economic** – the ability of an economy to meet present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland wording).
- **Environmental** – the ability of the environment to **support human life and well-being in the long term**.
- **Social** – the ability of society to meet its members' needs and ensure everyone can lead a **healthy, productive and fulfilling life**.

The **Venn diagram** (IUCN) shows the pairwise overlaps:
- Social ∩ Environment = **Bearable**
- Social ∩ Economic = **Equitable**
- Environment ∩ Economic = **Viable**
- All three = **Sustainable**

Important nuance from slide 15: the environment is not just an equal circle – it is **foundational**; societies and economies depend on it and must operate **within planetary boundaries**. This "nested" view leads directly to **Doughnut Economics** (slide 14) and to W2's planetary boundaries. The three dimensions also map onto the SDGs (W5) and their synergies/trade-offs (W7).
nodes.examTips: Classic question: name the 3 dimensions and the three overlaps (bearable = social+environment, equitable = social+economic, viable = environment+economic). Contrast the overlapping-circles model with the nested view (environment as foundation). Quiz 1: the ENVIRONMENT dimension is the foundation; society and economy must operate within planetary boundaries.

nodes.label: Doughnut Economics
nodes.summary: Kate Raworth's model: a safe and just space between a social foundation (inner ring) and an ecological ceiling (outer ring, planetary boundaries).
nodes.details:
**Doughnut Economics** (Kate Raworth) pictures the goal of an economy as a ring:

- **Outer circle – Ecological ceiling**: living within our means, minimising harm to the natural environment, maximising ecological benefit. Its segments are the **planetary boundaries**: climate change, ocean acidification, chemical pollution, nitrogen & phosphorus loading, freshwater withdrawals, land conversion, biodiversity loss, air pollution, ozone layer depletion. Red wedges beyond the ring = **overshoot**.
- **Inner circle – Social foundation**: addressing shortfalls and meeting needs, creating opportunity for all – water, food, health, education, income & work, peace & justice, political voice, social equity, gender equality, housing, networks, energy. Red wedges inside = **shortfall**.
- **The centre (the doughnut itself) – our aim**: the "sweet spot" where the needs of all are met while respecting the limits of the environment – the **safe and just space** for humanity.

Why it matters: it combines the biophysical **planetary boundaries** (W2) with SDG-like social minimums (W5), making clear that sustainability fails both by *overshoot* and by *deprivation* – relevant to the Global North/South debate (W4).
nodes.examTips: Know which ring is which: outer = ecological ceiling (planetary boundaries), inner = social foundation. Overshoot vs shortfall. Compare with the three-pillar Venn: the doughnut treats the environment as a hard limit.

nodes.label: Environment as foundation
nodes.summary: The environment is everything around us, living and non-living; it is foundational, so society and economy must operate within planetary boundaries.
nodes.details:
Slide 15 defines the **environment** as *everything around us*: all **living things** (plants, animals) and **non-living things** (air, water, sunlight) that interact with us.

Key claims:
- The environment is **foundational** – societies and economies depend on it and must operate **within planetary boundaries**. This is a stronger statement than the three equal pillars.
- A key component of **environmental science** is **ecology**, the study of ecosystems.
- The slide's figure (Miller & Spoolman 2019) shows the main **biotic** (living) and **abiotic** (non-living) components of an ecosystem – e.g. producers, consumers, decomposers; sunlight, water, CO2/O2, nutrients.

This node is the scientific bridge between the *idea* of sustainability and *why* human impacts matter: if the environment is the base, damaging it undermines the social and economic dimensions built on it.

nodes.label: Ecosystem
nodes.summary: Functional unit of a biotic community and its abiotic environment, linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling; from a log to the biosphere.
nodes.details:
An **ecosystem** is a **functional unit** consisting of a **community of living organisms (biotic)** and their **environment (abiotic)**, interacting and connected through **energy flow** and **nutrient cycling** (slide 15).

Scale (slide 16):
- It can be large – a **lake, forest or island** – or tiny – the space **beneath a fallen log** or a **desert spring**.
- Examples pictured: an aquatic coral-reef ecosystem (Papua New Guinea) and a terrestrial desert ecosystem (Namib).
- Many ecologists see the whole **biosphere** as a **global ecosystem** – the sum of all local ecosystems.

Consequences:
- The Earth's surface is a **network of interconnected ecosystems**.
- **Any activity** within an ecosystem affects its processes (**material cycles and energy flows**).

This interconnectedness underpins the first two **laws of ecology** and explains why local actions can add up to global changes – the logic behind **planetary boundaries** (W2) and **ecosystem services** (W4).
nodes.examTips: Define an ecosystem with all four parts: biotic community + abiotic environment + energy flow + nutrient cycling. Quiz 1: ecosystem (not biosphere, population or habitat) = biotic community + abiotic environment in energy flow and nutrient cycles.

nodes.label: Human activities alter ecosystems
nodes.summary: All human activities (forest clearing, fishing, logging) alter energy flows and nutrient/water cycles, changing ecosystem structure and the functions society relies on.
nodes.details:
Slide 17 (framed under the **social** dimension) states that **ultimately all activities impact the ecosystem/environment** we live in.

Examples given:
- **Clearing forest land for agriculture**
- **Fishing at sea**
- **Cutting trees for timber**

Mechanism (the key sentence to remember): human activities **alter energy flows and nutrient/water cycles** → this **changes the structure of ecosystems** → which ultimately **shifts the ecosystem functions that support society and the economy**.

So the chain is: *activity → process disruption → structural change → loss of functions → feedback on people*. This is the conceptual seed for:
- W2's **natural capital degradation** and **planetary boundaries** (land-system change, freshwater, biogeochemical flows);
- W4's **ecosystem services** (the "functions that support society").

nodes.label: Laws of ecology
nodes.summary: Six laws: everything is connected; species depend on each other; everything must go somewhere; thermodynamics applies; nature knows best; no free lunch.
nodes.details:
Slide 18 lists six **laws of ecology** (the first four and the last echo Barry Commoner's classic "four laws"):

1. **Every element is connected to everything else** – ecosystems are networks; disturbing one part ripples through.
2. **Every species depends on every other species** – interdependence within food webs.
3. **Everything must go somewhere** – matter is not destroyed; waste and pollution are just moved (e.g. plastics, CO2, fertiliser runoff).
4. **The laws of thermodynamics apply** – energy is conserved but degrades at each transfer; ecosystems need continuous energy input (sunlight).
5. **Nature knows best** – human interventions in natural systems are likely to be harmful; long-evolved systems are hard to improve.
6. **There is no such thing as a free lunch** – every gain from nature has a cost somewhere; exploitation always has consequences.

These laws give scientific weight to sustainability: e.g. law 3 explains pollution and the need for recycling (W7); law 6 explains why overconsumption has hidden costs (W3) and why planetary boundaries exist (W2).

**Quiz 1 link:** the lecturer pairs law 3 ("Everything must go somewhere") with the **laws of thermodynamics** (conservation: nothing disappears, it only changes place or form). On the slide the thermodynamics law is listed separately as law 4, so answer "thermodynamics" when asked what science principle law 3 relates to.
nodes.examTips: Be able to list the laws and illustrate one with a real example (e.g. 'everything must go somewhere' → microplastics, fertiliser runoff causing eutrophication). Quiz 1: "Everything must go somewhere" is the law the lecturer links closely to thermodynamics (matter is conserved, waste is only moved). Other options seen: Nature Knows Best, Everything is Connected to Everything Else, There is No Such Free Lunch; also "energy flow", "carrying capacity", "biodiversity" as lookalikes.

nodes.label: Part 2 · Environmental ethics
nodes.summary: Ethical theories about humans and nature, from the Dominion thesis and anthropocentrism to Leopold's ecocentric Land Ethic, applied to livestock and dam dilemmas.
nodes.details:
The second half covers **environmental ethics** (slide 9 outline): an illustration (**animal agriculture**), the **Dominion thesis and related theories**, and **conservation dilemma scenarios**.

A useful way to organise the theories is a **spectrum of moral concern**:

- **Human-centred (anthropocentric)**: Dominion thesis → Locke (nature as property) → anthropocentrism / utilitarianism → Pinchot's **conservationism** ("greatest good for the greatest number").
- **Middle ground**: **Stewardship** – humans have a moral responsibility to protect the environment and living things.
- **Nature-centred**: Muir's **preservationism** (non-utilitarian protection for wildlife) → Leopold's **Land Ethic** → **ecocentrism** (ecological interests above human interests).

The **Hetch Hetchy** dispute (Pinchot vs Muir) and the closing **dam-vs-salmon dilemma** force students to apply these positions to real trade-offs between economic benefit and ecological/indigenous values. This links to CPMK 4 (applying ethics in decisions).

nodes.label: Livestock industry: farrowing crates
nodes.summary: Farrowing crates confine sows to raise piglet survival and profit; opponents argue animals are sentient (A) or that industry harms small farms and water (B).
nodes.details:
The ethics section opens with a provocation: **how do you view the efficiency of the livestock industry?** (slide 21)

**Farrowing crates** are metal-barred crates in pig barns housing pregnant sows from just before birth until **30–35 days postpartum**. They **restrict the sow's movement**; they are considered **more economical** because they reduce accidental piglet deaths (crushing), increasing production and returns.

**Opponents of agricultural industrialisation** (slide 22) give two kinds of argument:
- **Argument A** – animals are not "capital" but **sentient beings**.
- **Argument B** – industrial livestock **shuts down small/traditional farms** and **pollutes water**, potentially harming **human health downstream**.

Both are **ethical** arguments (ethics = the branch of philosophy asking what is right and wrong; morality), but they differ: **Argument B is anthropocentric** (wrong because it harms *humans*), while **Argument A is non-anthropocentric** (wrong because of harm to the *animals themselves*).

Lesson: the same practice can be criticised from different moral standpoints – distinguishing *whose* interests count is the core skill of environmental ethics.
nodes.examTips: Likely question: which argument is anthropocentric? Answer: B (harm to farmers and downstream human health). A is non-anthropocentric (animal sentience).

nodes.label: What ethics is & its role
nodes.summary: Ethics is the branch of philosophy asking what is right or wrong; codes of conduct guided civilisations; Western ethics focuses on actions' impacts on others.
nodes.details:
**Ethics** = the branch of philosophy that questions **what is right and what is wrong**; **morality** (slide 22).

**Role of ethics** (slide 23):
- Throughout history, **codes of conduct** – including philosophies and religions – have guided civilisations.
- In the **"Western" ethical tradition**, the focus is on **one's actions and their impact on others**.

**Environmental ethics** asks the follow-up question: *who counts as "others"?* Only humans (now or in the future)? Animals? Whole ecosystems and "the land"? Each theory in this module answers differently:
- Dominion thesis / anthropocentrism – only humans count.
- Stewardship – humans are responsible for caring for nature.
- Land Ethic / ecocentrism – the moral community extends to soils, waters, plants and animals.

This framing also connects to Brundtland's **future generations** – an ethical extension across time.

nodes.label: Dominion thesis
nodes.summary: Humans are the pinnacle of creation, superior to and separate from nature, free to use it as they wish; nature valued only for human use.
nodes.details:
The **Dominion thesis** (slide 24) holds that:

- **Humans are the pinnacle of creation**, and therefore have the **ethical freedom to use nature in any way they deem beneficial**.
- Humans are a **separate and superior entity** to nature and its contents.
- **Nature is only useful as long as it benefits humans** – it has no value of its own.

**Historical illustration:** the **17th-century wolf eradication programme** – among the **first environmental regulations passed in North America** – aimed to wipe out a species seen as a threat to human interests (livestock), showing how early "environmental" law reflected dominion rather than protection.

Position on the spectrum: the most **extreme human-centred** view. It provides the backdrop against which the later theories react – **stewardship** reframes dominion as responsibility; **preservationism** and the **Land Ethic** reject human superiority altogether.
nodes.examTips: Contrast Dominion (humans above nature, nature has only instrumental value) with Stewardship (responsibility to care) and Ecocentrism (humans as plain members of the land community). Quiz 1: Dominion Thesis = humans separate from and superior to nature; nature useful only insofar as it benefits humans. Distractors: Utilitarianism, Land Ethic, Conservationism, Stewardship.

nodes.label: Human-centred theories
nodes.summary: Theories related to the Dominion thesis: Locke's nature-as-property, anthropocentrism, utilitarianism, and the softer stewardship ethic.
nodes.details:
Slides 25–26 present theories **related to the Dominion thesis**, which share a focus on human interests:

- **John Locke** – liberalism; limited government protecting **individual liberty and property rights**; nature as useful **"property"** for humans.
- **Anthropocentrism** – humans are the primary factor in judging whether actions toward nature are right or wrong.
- **Utilitarianism** – value is measured by **benefits** (maximising individual/societal welfare).
- **Stewardship** – a **moral responsibility to protect** the environment and living things; still centred on human agency, but as caretakers rather than owners.

These ideas are not just history: modern tools such as **economic valuation of ecosystem services** and **cost–benefit analysis** of projects (W4) are essentially **utilitarian and anthropocentric**. Pinchot's conservationism (next group) applies utilitarianism to resource management.

nodes.label: John Locke: nature as property
nodes.summary: Founder of liberalism: limited government to protect individual liberty and property rights; nature treated as useful property for humans.
nodes.details:
**John Locke** (17th-century English philosopher) is presented as a theory related to the Dominion thesis (slide 25):

- **Foundation of liberalism**.
- **Trust the government, but limited** – its role is to protect **individual liberty**, expressed especially through **property rights**.
- **Nature as utility** – a useful **"property"** for humans; land becomes valuable when people work it and own it.

Why it matters for sustainability:
- It explains the modern idea that **privatising** a resource gives owners an incentive to care for it – an argument that returns in W2 as one proposed fix for the **tragedy of the commons** (with limits: the atmosphere and high seas cannot be privatised).
- It reinforces an **instrumental** view of nature: nature's value is what it provides to owners.

Locke thus links the Dominion thesis to **anthropocentrism** and **utilitarianism** in a political-economic form.

nodes.label: Anthropocentrism
nodes.summary: Ethical viewpoint in which humans are the primary factor in deciding whether actions toward nature are right or wrong.
nodes.details:
**Anthropocentrism** (slide 25) is the ethical viewpoint that **humans are the primary factor in determining whether actions toward nature are right or wrong**.

- Nature matters **because of what it does for people** – food, water, health, livelihoods, beauty.
- An action harming nature is wrong *if and because* it harms humans (now or in the future).
- Example from this module: **Argument B** against industrial livestock (water pollution harms people downstream; small farmers lose livelihoods) is anthropocentric.

Anthropocentrism is not necessarily anti-environment: Brundtland's sustainable development, Pinchot's conservationism and ecosystem-service valuation are all broadly anthropocentric yet support protecting nature.

Its opposite is **ecocentrism** (Leopold): ecological interests come *above* human interests. Exam essays often ask you to place a viewpoint or argument on this **anthropocentric ↔ ecocentric** axis.
nodes.examTips: Most common compare/contrast: anthropocentrism vs ecocentrism. Give an example argument for each (e.g. dam for electricity/jobs vs protecting salmon and the ecosystem). Quiz 1: anthropocentrism = humans as the primary factor in judging right/wrong actions toward nature; distractors: ecocentrism, stewardship, utilitarianism, Land Ethic, preservationism.

nodes.label: Utilitarianism
nodes.summary: Normative ethical theory that judges value by benefits, aiming to maximise individual or societal welfare.
nodes.details:
**Utilitarianism** (slide 25) is a **normative ethical theory** that determines the **value of something by its benefits** – the right action is the one that **maximises individual/societal welfare**.

In environmental decisions:
- Nature is valued for the **welfare** it produces (resources, services, recreation).
- Choices are made by weighing total benefits against costs – the logic of **cost–benefit analysis**.
- **Gifford Pinchot** applied it to resource management: "**the greatest good for the greatest number**" (slide 27).
- In the **Hetch Hetchy** debate the utilitarian case was that the **dam gives greater benefits to society** (water supply).

Limitations to discuss: whose welfare is counted (future generations? animals? indigenous minorities?), and things that are hard to price (biodiversity, sacred places). **John Muir** is explicitly described as **non-utilitarian**, which makes Pinchot vs Muir the textbook contrast.

nodes.label: Stewardship
nodes.summary: The moral responsibility to protect the environment and living things; humans as caretakers rather than owners of nature.
nodes.details:
**Stewardship** (slide 26) = the **moral responsibility to protect the environment and living things**.

- Humans still hold a special position, but as **caretakers/trustees** rather than masters: we are *responsible for* nature, not merely entitled to use it.
- Often framed religiously or culturally (e.g. caring for creation, custodianship), and practically through everyday actions – the slide shows children recycling.
- It softens the **Dominion thesis**: same human agency, opposite moral direction (care instead of exploitation).
- It sits between **anthropocentrism** (nature for us) and **ecocentrism** (nature for its own sake).

Links: stewardship underlies community-based resource management – e.g. indigenous communities guarding customary forests (W2 Barambang Katute) – and the ethical responsibilities of individuals, corporations and governments discussed for **planetary boundaries** (W2 discussion).

nodes.label: Conservation vs preservation
nodes.summary: Pinchot's utilitarian conservationism (wise use) versus Muir's non-utilitarian preservationism, clashing over the Hetch Hetchy dam.
nodes.details:
Two founders of the US environmental movement represent opposite answers to *why protect nature?*

| | **Gifford Pinchot** | **John Muir** |
|---|---|---|
| Label | **Conservationist** | **Preservationist** |
| Aim | **Efficient and sustainable use** of natural resources | **Protection and preservation**, for the benefit of **wildlife** |
| Ethic | Utilitarian: "greatest good for the greatest number" | **Non-utilitarian** |
| Legacy | Enemy of the 'timber barons' (wasteful exploitation) | Pioneer of **national/conservation parks** in the US |

The clash came to a head over the **Hetch Hetchy Valley** dam (slide 29).

Key distinction for the exam: **conservation = wise use** (nature as a resource to manage sustainably); **preservation = protection from use** (nature valued for itself). Both oppose reckless exploitation, so both differ from the Dominion thesis – but only preservation moves away from anthropocentrism toward the **Land Ethic**.
nodes.examTips: Do not mix up conservation (Pinchot, use wisely) and preservation (Muir, protect from use). Expect a question applying both to a dam/forest scenario.

nodes.label: Gifford Pinchot: conservationism
nodes.summary: Conservationist favouring efficient, sustainable resource use for 'the greatest good for the greatest number'; opponent of the timber barons.
nodes.details:
**Gifford Pinchot** (first chief of the US Forest Service) – slide 27:

- **Conservationist** → advocates the **efficient and sustainable use of natural resources**.
- Motto: **"the greatest good for the greatest number"** – an explicit application of **utilitarianism** to nature.
- **Enemy of the 'timber baron'** – opposed private loggers who stripped forests for quick profit, arguing forests should be managed scientifically so they keep producing for society long-term.

Interpretation:
- Nature is a **resource** whose value lies in **human use**, but use must be **sustained** – very close to Carlowitz's sustainable forestry (1713) and to the economic reading of Brundtland.
- In the **Hetch Hetchy** dispute Pinchot backed the dam because it provided **greater benefits to society** (water for San Francisco).

Pinchot shows that **anthropocentric** ethics can still be pro-conservation – the debate with Muir is about *why* and *how much* to protect, not whether.
keyTerms: greatest good for the greatest number

nodes.label: John Muir: preservationism
nodes.summary: Preservationist, non-utilitarian: manage nature primarily for protection and wildlife; pioneer of US conservation (national) parks.
nodes.details:
**John Muir** (naturalist, founder of the Sierra Club) – slide 28:

- **Preservationist**.
- Natural resources should be managed **primarily for protection and preservation**, **for the benefit of wildlife** rather than human consumption.
- **Non-utilitarian** – nature's value is not reducible to its usefulness to people.
- **Pioneer of conservation parks** in the United States (e.g. Yosemite).

In the **Hetch Hetchy** dispute Muir opposed the dam: the valley was a **biodiversity 'treasure'**, and the dam would **disrupt wildlife** (slide 29).

Muir's position moves toward **non-anthropocentric** ethics and prefigures Leopold's **Land Ethic** and ecocentrism. In modern terms, protected areas and biodiversity strategies (e.g. W5's IBSAP, SDG 15) carry this preservationist strand.
nodes.examTips: Quiz 1: John Muir = preservationist, protection of wilderness for its own sake, NON-utilitarian (not Pinchot, Malthus, Locke). The quiz spells Pinchot "Clifford"; the slide says Gifford.

nodes.label: Hetch Hetchy Valley dam
nodes.summary: Pinchot vs Muir: the dam brings greater benefits to society versus the valley as a biodiversity treasure whose wildlife the dam would disrupt.
nodes.details:
**Hetch Hetchy Valley** (in Yosemite National Park, California) was the site of a famous early-20th-century dispute over damming the valley to supply water to San Francisco (the dam was approved in 1913).

The slide frames it as **Pinchot vs Muir**:
- **Pinchot (conservationist, utilitarian):** the **dam provides greater benefits to society** – reliable water and power for many people.
- **Muir (preservationist, non-utilitarian):** the valley is a **biodiversity 'treasure'**, and the **dam disrupts wildlife**.

Why it is taught:
- It is the classic real-world test of **conservation vs preservation**, and of **utilitarian/anthropocentric** vs **nature-centred** reasoning.
- The same structure reappears in the module's final **conservation dilemma** (dam vs migratory salmon and indigenous livelihoods) and in modern infrastructure debates in Indonesia (dams, mining, food estates) – classic **trade-offs** between SDGs (W7).
nodes.examTips: Use Hetch Hetchy as an illustration when asked to contrast conservationism and preservationism. Quiz 1: Muir opposed the dam because it would disturb wilderness and biodiversity; Pinchot (conservationism) wanted efficient use for the greatest benefit of society. Muir is NOT the utilitarian.

nodes.label: Aldo Leopold: Land Ethic
nodes.summary: Land is not mere property; moral community extended to soils, waters, plants and animals—humans as 'plain member and citizen', not conqueror.
nodes.details:
**Aldo Leopold**'s **"Land Ethic"** (*A Sand County Almanac*, 1949) – slide 30:

- **Land is not just 'property'** – a direct challenge to Locke and the Dominion thesis.
- Builds on the idea of **interdependence in society**: to survive and belong to a community, individuals **voluntarily give up absolute freedom**.
- Leopold **stretches the boundary of dependency** to include **nature and other living things** – the community now includes soils, waters, plants and animals ("the land").
- This is a **moral extension**: "we must change our relationship with nature… **from conqueror… to plain member and citizen**" (Leopold, 1949).

The Land Ethic leads to **ecocentrism** (child node), the far nature-centred end of the spectrum.

Connections: echoes the **laws of ecology** (everything connected, species interdependent) and **stewardship**; it also resonates with indigenous/customary relationships to land such as the **Barambang Katute customary forest** (W2).
nodes.examTips: Remember the quote 'from conqueror to plain member and citizen' and the idea of moral extension. Leopold → ecocentrism; Dominion → anthropocentrism.

nodes.label: Ecocentrism
nodes.summary: Ecological interests must be placed above the interests of the human species when judging whether an action is right or wrong.
nodes.details:
**Ecocentrism** (slide 30): **ecological interests must be above the interests of the human species** in determining whether an action is right or wrong.

- The moral reference point is the **whole ecosystem** (species, processes, the land community), not individual humans.
- An action is right if it preserves the **integrity, stability and health** of the ecological community – even if it costs humans something.
- It is the **opposite of anthropocentrism** and goes further than stewardship (which keeps humans in charge).

Applying it:
- In the **dam-vs-salmon dilemma**, an ecocentric view would reject a dam that destroys the salmon migration and the watershed, regardless of the electricity and jobs.
- In the **livestock case**, it supports concern for animals and ecosystems, not just downstream human health.

Ecocentric thinking also underlies **planetary boundaries** thinking about Earth-system integrity (W2), though that framework itself is justified by human welfare.
nodes.examTips: Pair with anthropocentrism. Be able to say which stance each actor in a dilemma takes (company/government vs environmentalists/indigenous community). Quiz 1: ecological interests override human-species interests when judging the morality of an action = ecocentrism (not anthropocentrism, utilitarianism, Dominion Thesis).

nodes.label: Conservation dilemma: dam vs salmon
nodes.summary: An energy company's dam brings electricity and jobs but threatens migratory salmon and an indigenous community; the government supports it, environmentalists oppose.
nodes.details:
**Scenario** (slide 31): an **energy company** proposes a **dam**. It would bring significant **economic benefits** – national electricity supply, employment and more. But the **watershed** is crucial for **migratory salmon**, and is home to small **indigenous communities** who have depended on salmon for generations. The dam would block migration routes, **sharply reduce salmon** and **disrupt indigenous ways of life**. The **government supports** it (fits regional/national growth plans); **environmentalists and some indigenous members strongly oppose** it.

**Model answer outline:**
- **Identify stakeholders and their ethics**: company & government – utilitarian/anthropocentric (greatest good, growth); environmentalists – preservationist/ecocentric; indigenous community – livelihood, cultural rights, often stewardship/land-ethic relationship to place.
- **Apply theories**: Pinchot would weigh total benefits; Muir/Leopold would protect the watershed; stewardship asks what responsible care requires.
- **Sustainability dimensions**: economic gain vs environmental integrity vs social justice (who bears the costs?).
- **Possible ways forward**: free, prior and informed consent of indigenous people, fish passages or alternative sites/energy sources, compensation and benefit-sharing, cumulative impact assessment.
- Conclude with a reasoned position that acknowledges the **trade-off**.
nodes.examTips: Structure answers: stakeholders → ethical stance of each → dimension conflicts → options → your justified position.

nodes.label: W2 · Tragedy of the Commons & Planetary Boundaries
nodes.summary: Week 2: Hardin's tragedy of the commons, commons vs open access, community-managed examples, and the planetary boundaries framework with its 2025 status.
nodes.details:
Week 2 ("Tragedy of the Commons and the Impact of Human Activities on the Environment") has two parts:

- **Part 1 – Tragedy of the commons.** Garrett **Hardin (1968)**: an open pasture where each herder adds cattle leads inevitably to ruin. The lecture then challenges Hardin: true **commons** are jointly owned with defined members and exclusion, unlike **open-access resources** (atmosphere, high seas). Community-managed cases – **Barambang Katute customary forest** and **Maine lobster fisheries** – show the tragedy lies in **unmanaged open access**, not in sharing itself.
- **Part 2 – Planetary boundaries.** The Earth-system framework (Rockström et al. 2009) identifies **nine processes** that keep the planet stable and defines a **safe operating space for humanity**. As of the **2025 update, 7 of 9 boundaries are transgressed** – only stratospheric ozone and atmospheric aerosol loading remain safe. Slides illustrate land use, water, climate, biodiversity, biogeochemical flows and chemical pollution, plus **natural capital degradation** on land and sea, and end with discussion questions.

The link between the halves: the Earth system's sinks and cycles are the ultimate **global open-access commons**, so crossing planetary boundaries is the tragedy of the commons at planetary scale.

nodes.label: Part 1 · Tragedy of the commons
nodes.summary: Hardin's argument, the commons vs open-access distinction, and community-managed counter-examples showing that management regimes, not sharing, decide the outcome.
nodes.details:
Structure of Part 1 (slides 2–5):

1. **Hardin's tragedy** – shared, open resources are degraded because each user reasons that their small extra use or pollution won't matter; cumulatively, everyone loses.
2. **Commons vs open access** – Hardin's "commons" is debated: in the literature *commons* means **shared ownership** by a defined community with exclusion of non-members. Tragedy happens in **open-access resources that are not well managed**.
3. **Open-access resources** – owned by no one, usable by almost anyone: the **atmosphere** and the **open sea** and its fish; partly-open shared resources include grasslands, forests, rivers and aquifers.
4. **Does the tragedy lie in the commons?** – No: the **Barambang Katute** customary forest and **Maine lobster** fisheries show communities with rules can sustain shared resources.
5. **Solutions** – reduce use by agreement, regulate access, or privatise (which fails for the atmosphere and high seas).

Key message: *the problem is the management regime, not sharing itself.*

nodes.label: Hardin's Tragedy of the Commons (1968)
nodes.summary: Hardin (Science, 1968): on a pasture open to all, each herder adds cattle for private gain while costs are shared, ruining the resource.
nodes.details:
**Garrett Hardin**, "The Tragedy of the Commons", *Science*, **1968** (slide 2; the speaker notes mistakenly say 1986).

> "Picture a pasture that is open to all. Each herdsman will try to keep as many cattle as possible on the commons… the inherent logic of the commons remorselessly generates tragedy."

Hardin's "commons" = a resource **open to all (open access)**.

**The logic** (from the lecturer's notes): degradation of shared or open-access **renewable** resources happens because each user thinks, *"the little I use or pollute won't matter – and it's renewable anyway."* At low use this seems true. But the **cumulative impact** of many users exploiting a widely available resource **degrades, depletes or destroys** it. In the end **no one benefits and everyone loses** – that is the tragedy.

Underlying mechanism: **benefits are private** (each extra cow earns the herder money) while **costs are shared** by all (overgrazing) – an **externality**.

Examples of the pattern today: overfishing on the high seas, groundwater depletion, air pollution, and greenhouse-gas emissions into the shared atmosphere (W6).
nodes.examTips: Explain the private-benefit / shared-cost logic. Hardin published in Science in 1968 (not 1986). Know the critique: his 'commons' is really open access.

nodes.label: Commons vs open-access resource
nodes.summary: Commons: joint ownership by a bounded community that excludes non-members. Open access: no ownership rights, the whole public, no exclusion.
nodes.details:
Hardin's use of "commons" is **debated**, because in the literature **commons refers to shared ownership** (slide 3). The comparison table:

| | **The commons** | **Open-access resource** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ownership** | **Joint ownership** | **No ownership rights or possession** |
| **Community** | A group defined and restricted more narrowly, with **clear boundaries between members and non-members** | The **community at large** |
| **Exclusion** | **Non-members excluded** | **None** |

**Conclusion of the slide:** the distinction emphasises that **tragedy can occur in open-access resources that are not well managed**. A true commons, with its own members, rules and exclusion, can be used sustainably.

This is the key correction to Hardin (associated in the wider literature with Elinor Ostrom's work on common-pool resource institutions). It sets up the counter-examples on slide 5 and W4's discussion of commons in the Global South and how commons are regulated.
nodes.examTips: A favourite exam item: fill in or explain the 3-row table (ownership, community, exclusion). Say clearly: tragedy = unmanaged open access, not common property.

nodes.label: Open-access resources
nodes.summary: Renewable resources owned by no one and usable by almost anyone, e.g. the atmosphere and open sea; grasslands, forests, rivers, aquifers are often shared.
nodes.details:
Slide 4: some **renewable resources**, known as **open-access resources**, are **not owned by anyone** and **can be used by almost anyone**.

**Fully open-access examples:**
- The **atmosphere** (a sink for CO2 and air pollutants)
- The **open sea** and its **fish**

**Not entirely open, but often used collectively:**
- **Grasslands**
- **Forests**
- **Rivers**
- **Underground water bodies (aquifers)**

Why it matters:
- These are exactly the resources most at risk of a Hardin-style tragedy, because nobody can exclude others and no one bears the full cost of overuse.
- The truly global ones (atmosphere, high seas) **cannot be divided and sold as private property**, so privatisation is not a solution – they need **collective agreements** (e.g. international treaties such as the Montreal Protocol for ozone, W4, or the Paris Agreement for climate, W6).
- Several of them correspond to planetary boundaries: climate change (atmosphere), ocean acidification (open sea), freshwater change (rivers, aquifers), land-system change (forests).
nodes.examTips: Quiz 1: "renewable resources owned by no one, usable by almost anyone, e.g. atmosphere, open ocean" = Open-Access Resources (not The Commons, not private property, not ecosystem services).

nodes.label: Does the tragedy lie in the commons?
nodes.summary: No: the tragedy comes from unmanaged open access. Commons with boundaries, rules, monitoring and sanctions often stay sustainable.
nodes.details:
Slide 5 asks **"Does the tragedy lie in the commons?"** The lecturer's answer (notes): **the tragedy is not in the commons but in unmanaged open access.**

- Hardin mainly described **open access** – no rights, rules or monitoring – not **common property** managed by a community.
- Many commons stay **sustainable** when they have: **clear boundaries**, **harvest rules/quotas**, **monitoring**, **graduated sanctions**, and **forums for resolving disputes**.
- What usually triggers "tragedy": **absence of institutions**, **high monitoring costs**, **externalities** (costs spread onto the public), and **mismatch of scale** – e.g. the **atmosphere as a global commons**.
- Contrast: coastal fisheries under **customary (adat) rules** are often more sustainable than the **open high seas**, where overfishing is easy.

**So the problem is the management regime – not sharing resources itself.**

Examples on the slide: **Barambang Katute customary forest** and **Maine lobster fisheries** (children).
nodes.examTips: If asked 'is Hardin right?', answer: partly – for unmanaged open access; but community commons with rules (Barambang Katute, Maine lobsters) avoid the tragedy. List the institutional ingredients. Quiz 1: managed commons (Barambang Katute, Maine lobster) avoid tragedy because of mechanisms of policy and boundaries applied by the local community; unmanaged = Hardin 1968 assumption.

nodes.label: Barambang Katute customary forest
nodes.summary: Indonesian customary (adat) forest managed by the Barambang Katute indigenous community, with protection mechanisms and sacred areas where mining is banned.
nodes.details:
**Example 2** on slide 5: the **customary forest (hutan adat) of Barambang Katute** (Sinjai, South Sulawesi, Indonesia).

- The forest is **managed by the Barambang Katute indigenous community**.
- The community has **mechanisms in place to protect** the forest area.
- There are **sacred areas where mining is not allowed**.

Why it matters:
- It is a **true commons** in the sense of slide 3: **joint ownership** by a **defined community** with rules that **exclude** harmful uses and outsiders.
- Customary rules and sacred zoning function as the **institutions** (boundaries, rules, enforcement) that prevent Hardin's tragedy – showing the problem is **unmanaged open access**, not shared ownership.
- It is a local, Indonesian illustration of **indigenous stewardship** and of a land-ethic-like relationship to place (W1), and of how **commons in the Global South** are often governed by customary institutions (W4).

Contrast: if the same forest were treated as open access or opened to mining without community control, it would be vulnerable to degradation.
nodes.examTips: Use as the Indonesian example of a well-managed commons. Point to the protection mechanisms and sacred no-mining areas as the 'rules' that prevent tragedy.

nodes.label: Maine lobster fisheries
nodes.summary: Local lobster-fishing communities in Maine use shared policy mechanisms to protect waters and lobster stocks and avoid overfishing.
nodes.details:
**Example 1** on slide 5: **lobster fisheries in Maine** (the slide says "UK", but Maine is in the north-eastern **USA**).

- Local communities have **policy mechanisms among themselves** to **protect water resources and lobsters** and to **avoid overfishing**.
- In practice such systems involve informal territories ("harbor gangs"), limits on traps and catches, and protecting egg-bearing females – a classic case in commons research.

Lesson: a fishery – normally a textbook open-access tragedy – can be sustained when the users form a **bounded community with rules, monitoring and sanctions**. It contrasts with the **open high seas**, where no one can exclude others and overfishing is common.

Together with Barambang Katute it shows the pattern holds for both **forests** and **fisheries**, and in both Global North and Global South settings.

nodes.label: Solutions to the tragedy
nodes.summary: Reduce use by agreement, regulate access, or privatise, though privatisation often fails and cannot apply to the atmosphere or high seas.
nodes.details:
From the lecturer's notes on slide 5, there are two broad ways to tackle the tragedy:

1. **Use the shared/open-access resource at a lower level** – by **mutually agreeing to reduce use**, **regulating access** to the resource, or **both**. Examples: quotas, seasons, licences, community rules, international treaties.
2. **Convert the shared resource into private property** – the argument (Locke-style, W1) is that **owners protect their investment**.
   - But **history shows this does not always happen** (owners may still over-exploit for short-term profit).
   - It **cannot be applied** to open-access resources like the **atmosphere** and **high seas**, which **cannot be divided and sold** as private property.

A third, implied route is **community-based common-property management** (Barambang Katute, Maine lobsters), which combines reduced use with regulated access by insiders.

These options reappear in W4 ("regulating commons": Montreal Protocol, Subak irrigation, emissions regulation) and W6 (Paris Agreement for the atmosphere).
nodes.examTips: Know why privatisation fails for global commons (atmosphere/high seas can't be divided) – hence international agreements are needed.

nodes.label: Part 2 · Planetary boundaries
nodes.summary: The nine planetary boundaries framework, its 2025 status (7 of 9 transgressed), the link to doughnut economics, human impacts on ecosystems, and discussion.
nodes.details:
Part 2 (slides 6–13) turns from local commons to the **whole Earth system**:

- **The framework** (slide 6): based on Earth system science; **nine processes** regulating planetary stability; a **safe operating space for humanity** (Rockström et al., *Nature* 461:472, 2009).
- **2025 status** (slide 7): **7 of 9 boundaries transgressed** – Earth is outside the safe operating space (Stockholm Resilience Centre, Sept 2025).
- **The nine boundaries** illustrated (slides 8–10): land-use change and global water cycle; climate change and biodiversity loss; biogeochemical flows (eutrophication) and chemical pollution; plus ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone and atmospheric aerosols from the diagram.
- **Doughnut economics** (notes, slide 7): planetary boundaries as the ecological ceiling.
- **Natural capital degradation** (slides 11–12): major human impacts on terrestrial and marine ecosystems (Miller & Spoolman 2019).
- **Discussion** (slide 13).

Key idea: human pressure on Earth's shared systems is the planetary version of the tragedy of the commons.

nodes.label: Planetary boundaries framework
nodes.summary: Earth-system framework identifying nine processes that regulate planetary stability and setting science-based limits: a safe operating space for humanity.
nodes.details:
The **planetary boundaries framework** (Rockström et al., *Nature* 461:472, **2009**; Stockholm Resilience Centre) – slide 6:

- Draws on **Earth system science**.
- Identifies **nine processes** critical for the **stability and resilience of the Earth system** as a whole.
- Delineates the **biophysical and biochemical systems and processes** that regulate the planet's state within ranges that are **historically known** and **scientifically likely** to keep the Earth system stable and its **life-support systems** conducive to human welfare and societal development.
- Formulates **limits to the impact of the anthroposphere** (human activity) on the Earth system, defining a **scientifically based safe operating space for humanity** that safeguards **Earth's interglacial state** (the stable Holocene climate in which civilisation developed) and its **resilience**.

How to read the diagrams: the **green inner zone = safe operating space**; wedges extending outward into yellow/orange/red = **increasing risk** of destabilising, possibly irreversible change.

The nine: **climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows (N, P), ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading, novel entities**.
nodes.examTips: Be able to name all nine boundaries and explain 'safe operating space'. Remember the boundaries are about Earth-system stability, not resource depletion per se. Quiz 1: purpose = identify scientifically based limits that define a SAFE OPERATING SPACE for humanity within the Earth system (not max GDP, not a fossil-fuel depletion date, not 2050 energy capacity).

nodes.label: Boundaries breached: 6 (quiz) vs 7 (2025 slide)
nodes.summary: Quiz key: 6 of 9 boundaries breached (outside the safe operating space). The 2025 slide update counts 7, adding ocean acidification.
nodes.details:
**Quiz 1 headline fact: 6 of the 9 boundaries are currently breached** (Q10, options 3 / 5 / 6 / 9; key = 6). The lecturer's key matches the 2023 update (Richardson et al.): climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows and novel entities. **Slide 7 (2025 update) shows 7**, because ocean acidification was newly crossed. If the options contain 6 and not 7, answer 6; if 7 is offered, 7 is the slide figure. 2009 diagram (slide 6): only 3 crossed.

Slide 7 (Stockholm Resilience Centre, **24 Sept 2025**; diagram "The 2025 update to the Planetary Boundaries", Sakschewski & Caesar et al. 2025): **7 out of 9 planetary boundaries have been transgressed**, meaning **Earth is now outside the safe operating space for humanity**.

**Transgressed (7):**
1. **Climate change** – both CO2 concentration and radiative forcing
2. **Biosphere integrity** – genetic and functional (functional in the high-risk red zone)
3. **Land-system change**
4. **Freshwater change** – blue water and green water
5. **Biogeochemical flows** – nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), both deep in the high-risk zone
6. **Novel entities** (synthetic chemicals, plastics etc.)
7. **Ocean acidification** – newly breached in the 2025 assessment

**Within the safe space (2):**
8. **Stratospheric ozone depletion**
9. **Atmospheric aerosol loading**

Compare the older 2009 diagram on slide 6: then only **3** were crossed (climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen cycle), and chemical pollution and aerosols were **"not yet quantified"**. The trend shows a rapidly worsening situation.
nodes.examTips: Quiz 1 key: 6 of 9 breached (=> outside the safe operating space). Slide 7 (2025) says 7 of 9; the 2 still safe are ozone and aerosols; ocean acidification is the newest crossed. 2009: 3. Ensure you can name the 6/7 and the safe ones.

nodes.label: The nine boundaries
nodes.summary: The nine Earth-system processes, grouped by 2025 status: seven transgressed and two still within the safe operating space.
nodes.details:
The nine planetary boundaries, grouped by **2025 status** (slide 7 diagram):

**Transgressed (outside safe operating space):**
- Climate change
- Biosphere integrity (biodiversity loss)
- Land-system change
- Freshwater change
- Biogeochemical flows (N & P)
- Novel entities (chemical pollution)
- Ocean acidification

**Safe (within safe operating space):**
- Stratospheric ozone depletion
- Atmospheric aerosol loading

Slides 8–10 illustrate six of them with photos and one-line explanations: **land-use change** and the **global water cycle** (slide 8), **climate change** and **biodiversity loss** (slide 9), **biogeochemical flows** (eutrophication) and **chemical pollution** (slide 10).

Memory aid – the boundaries are *interlinked*: e.g. deforestation (land) releases CO2 (climate), destroys habitat (biosphere) and alters rainfall (freshwater); fertiliser (N, P) causes eutrophication that harms aquatic biodiversity.
nodes.examTips: Practise listing all nine from memory, then sorting them into 7 breached / 2 safe.

nodes.label: Transgressed boundaries (7)
nodes.summary: Climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, novel entities and ocean acidification are beyond safe limits (2025).
nodes.details:
Seven boundaries are **outside the safe operating space** in the 2025 update (slide 7):

| Boundary | Sub-indicators on the diagram | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Climate change** | CO2 concentration; radiative forcing | high (radiative forcing red) |
| **Biosphere integrity** | genetic; functional | functional in high-risk red |
| **Land-system change** | – | increasing risk |
| **Freshwater change** | blue water; green water | increasing risk |
| **Biogeochemical flows** | phosphorus (P); nitrogen (N) | both high-risk red |
| **Novel entities** | – | far beyond boundary |
| **Ocean acidification** | – | just beyond boundary (newly crossed) |

The most severe overshoots are **biosphere integrity (functional)**, **biogeochemical flows (N, P)** and **novel entities**; climate change's radiative forcing is also in the high-risk zone.

The drivers are human activities discussed throughout the course: fossil fuels, agriculture and fertiliser, deforestation, irrigation, industrial chemicals and plastics – i.e. **overconsumption** and the **IPAT** drivers of W3.

nodes.label: Climate change
nodes.summary: GHG emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels, raise atmospheric CO2 and cause global warming; both CO2 concentration and radiative forcing are transgressed.
nodes.details:
**Climate change** (slide 9): **greenhouse-gas emissions**, particularly from **burning fossil fuels**, have **increased CO2 concentrations** in the atmosphere, causing **global warming and climate change**.

**Status 2025: transgressed.** The diagram shows two control variables, both beyond the boundary:
- **CO2 concentration** (the boundary is commonly set at **350 ppm**; current levels are well above 400 ppm).
- **Radiative forcing** – the extra energy trapped by greenhouse gases – in the **high-risk (red)** zone.

Why it matters:
- Climate is a **core boundary**: it interacts with almost all others (ocean acidification from the same CO2, biosphere stress, freshwater changes).
- The atmosphere is the classic **global open-access commons** – every emitter gains privately while the cost of warming is shared, a Hardin tragedy at planetary scale.
- W6 covers this in depth: greenhouse gases, the **Paris Agreement**, CBDR-RC and Indonesia's NDC.
nodes.examTips: Link climate change both to planetary boundaries (W2) and to the atmosphere as an open-access commons.

nodes.label: Biosphere integrity (biodiversity loss)
nodes.summary: Habitat destruction, pollution and exploitation drive extinctions at a very high rate; both genetic and functional diversity are transgressed, functional at high risk.
nodes.details:
**Loss of biodiversity / biosphere integrity** (slide 9): human activities such as **habitat destruction**, **pollution** and **resource exploitation** have caused **species extinction at a very high rate**, **disrupting ecosystem functions**.

**Status 2025: transgressed** on both sub-indicators:
- **Genetic diversity** – the variety of genes/species (measured via extinction rate).
- **Functional integrity** – the biosphere's capacity to keep ecosystems working (e.g. energy available to ecosystems); shown in the **high-risk red** zone.

In the 2009 diagram (slide 6) **biodiversity loss** was already the most extreme overshoot of all.

Why it matters: biodiversity underpins **ecosystem services** (pollination, food, clean water, climate regulation – W4) and ecosystem resilience. Its loss links to land-system change (habitat conversion), chemical pollution and climate change. Conservation responses include protected areas, Indonesia's **IBSAP** and SDGs 14 & 15 (W5).

nodes.label: Land-system change
nodes.summary: Large-scale conversion of land for agriculture, urbanisation and deforestation disrupts ecosystems, reduces biodiversity and alters carbon and water cycles. Transgressed.
nodes.details:
**Changes in land use** (slide 8): **large-scale land conversion** for **agriculture**, **urbanisation** and **deforestation** has **disrupted natural ecosystems**, **reduced biodiversity** and **affected carbon and water cycles**. (The slide's photo source discusses deforestation in Indonesia.)

**Status 2025: transgressed.** The control variable is essentially how much of the original **forest cover** remains (tropical, temperate and boreal forests regulate climate and water).

Connections:
- Directly drives **biosphere integrity** loss (habitat), **climate change** (CO2 from cleared forests and drained peat) and **freshwater change** (rainfall recycling).
- Indonesia is a key case: oil-palm expansion, peatland drainage and forest fires – covered in W6 (**peatlands**, **AFOLU** emissions).
- Mirrors W1's example of **clearing forest for agriculture** altering ecosystem functions.
nodes.examTips: Quiz 1: deforestation + urbanisation + agricultural expansion violate the LAND-SYSTEM CHANGE boundary (not freshwater, ocean acidification, ozone).

nodes.label: Freshwater change (global water cycle)
nodes.summary: Large-scale irrigation and river diversion alter the hydrological cycle, causing droughts, floods and poorer water quality; blue and green water both transgressed.
nodes.details:
**Global water cycle** (slide 8): changes in water use such as **large-scale irrigation** and **river diversion** have **altered the hydrological cycle**, causing **droughts, floods and a decline in water quality**.

**Status 2025: transgressed** for both sub-indicators on the diagram:
- **Blue water** – surface and groundwater in rivers, lakes and aquifers (what we withdraw for irrigation, industry and households).
- **Green water** – water held in soil and available to plants (affected by deforestation and land use).

In the 2009 diagram this was called "global freshwater use" and was still within the boundary; the updated framework ("freshwater change") shows it has been crossed.

Connections: water is a shared and often open-access resource (rivers, aquifers – slide 4); it is central to the **food–energy–water nexus** (W7) and to SDG 6; drought and floods also interact with climate change (W6).

nodes.label: Biogeochemical flows (N & P)
nodes.summary: Excess synthetic fertiliser sends nitrogen and phosphorus into ecosystems, causing eutrophication and disrupting natural cycles; both N and P are in the high-risk zone.
nodes.details:
**Biogeochemical flows** (slide 10): **excessive use of synthetic fertilisers** in agriculture has led to excess flows of **nitrogen (N)** and **phosphorus (P)** into ecosystems, causing **eutrophication** and disrupting natural nutrient cycles.

**Eutrophication** (pictured on the slide): nutrient runoff fertilises lakes, rivers and coasts → **algal blooms** → when algae die and decompose, oxygen is depleted → fish kills and "dead zones", plus poorer water quality.

**Status 2025: transgressed**, with **both N and P deep in the high-risk (red) zone** – among the most severely overshot boundaries. In the 2009 diagram the **nitrogen cycle** was already one of the three crossed.

Connections:
- Driven by industrial agriculture feeding a growing, richer population (W3 IPAT; W1 livestock case).
- Feeds into biosphere loss (aquatic ecosystems) and coral reef damage ("algae growth from fertiliser runoff", slide 12).
- An everyday example of W1's law **"everything must go somewhere"**; relevant to the **food** part of the FEW nexus (W7).
nodes.examTips: Explain the eutrophication chain: fertiliser runoff → algal bloom → oxygen depletion → dead zones. Quiz 1: synthetic-fertiliser N and P runoff causing eutrophication = BIOGEOCHEMICAL FLOWS (not climate change, chemical pollution/novel entities, land-system change).

nodes.label: Novel entities (chemical pollution)
nodes.summary: Hazardous chemicals—pesticides, heavy metals, industrial chemicals, plastics—pollute the environment and harm human and animal health; far beyond the boundary.
nodes.details:
**Chemical pollution / novel entities** (slide 10): the use of **hazardous chemicals**, including **pesticides**, **heavy metals** and **industrial chemicals**, has **polluted the environment**, affecting the **health of humans and animals**. (The slide's photo source refers to industrial – paper-mill – waste polluting the **Brantas river** basin in East Java.)

**Novel entities** is the current name for this boundary: new substances and materials created by humans that did not exist in nature – synthetic chemicals, **plastics**, pesticides, and modified life forms – released faster than they can be assessed or monitored.

**Status:** in **2009** it was "**not yet quantified**" (slide 6). In the **2025** diagram it is shown as **transgressed, extending far into the high-risk zone**.

Connections: plastics and waste link to W1's law "**everything must go somewhere**", the W2 discussion question on **reducing plastic use**, and recycling/circular solutions in W7.

nodes.label: Ocean acidification
nodes.summary: Oceans absorb CO2, lowering pH and harming shell- and reef-building organisms; newly transgressed in the 2025 update—the seventh boundary breached.
nodes.details:
**Ocean acidification** appears on both boundary diagrams (slides 6–7). Standard explanation: the ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of human CO2 emissions; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, **lowering seawater pH** and reducing the carbonate ions that corals, shellfish and plankton need to build shells and skeletons.

**Status:**
- **2009** (slide 6): within the safe space.
- **2025** (slide 7): **just beyond the boundary** – it is the boundary **newly breached** in the 2025 assessment, bringing the total to **7 of 9**.

Connections:
- Shares its driver with **climate change** (CO2 from fossil fuels).
- Harms **marine ecosystems and coral reefs**; slide 12 lists **"rising ocean acidity"** and **bleaching** among major human impacts on coral reefs.
- The open sea is an **open-access resource** (slide 4) – nobody owns it, so no single actor protects it.
- Relevant to SDG 14 (life below water, W5).
nodes.examTips: Remember ocean acidification is the 7th boundary crossed (2025) and shares the CO2 driver with climate change.

nodes.label: Boundaries still safe (2)
nodes.summary: Stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading remain within the safe operating space in the 2025 update.
nodes.details:
Only **two** of the nine boundaries remain **within the safe operating space** in the 2025 update (slide 7):

1. **Stratospheric ozone depletion** – recovering thanks to global action (Montreal Protocol).
2. **Atmospheric aerosol loading** – globally within the boundary, though regional pollution can be severe.

In the **2009** diagram (slide 6), ozone was within the boundary and aerosol loading was "**not yet quantified**".

Why this matters for the exam: the **ozone** case is the main **success story** – it shows that a global open-access commons problem (the atmosphere) *can* be solved when countries agree to **regulate access/reduce use** collectively, which is the solution logic from Part 1 and the "regulating commons" example in W4.
nodes.examTips: Name the two safe boundaries (ozone, aerosols) and use ozone/Montreal Protocol as proof global commons can be governed.

nodes.label: Stratospheric ozone depletion
nodes.summary: Thinning of the protective stratospheric ozone layer by ozone-depleting chemicals; within the safe space in 2025, recovering after the Montreal Protocol.
nodes.details:
**Stratospheric ozone depletion** appears on both diagrams (slides 6–7). Standard background: the ozone layer in the stratosphere filters harmful **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**. Synthetic chemicals such as **CFCs** (from refrigerants, aerosol sprays) destroyed ozone, creating the Antarctic "ozone hole".

**Status:** **within the safe operating space** in both 2009 and 2025. Recovery is credited to the **Montreal Protocol (1987)**, which phased out ozone-depleting substances worldwide.

Why it matters:
- It is the best example that a **planetary boundary can be pulled back** by coordinated international policy.
- It is a model for solving a **global open-access commons** problem (the atmosphere cannot be privatised, so collective rules are needed).
- Related: slide 12 lists **increased UV exposure** as a stress on coral reefs.
- Detailed further in W4 (**ozone / Montreal Protocol** as regulating the commons).

nodes.label: Atmospheric aerosol loading
nodes.summary: Fine particles from burning, industry and dust that affect climate, monsoons and health; within the safe space in 2025, 'not yet quantified' in 2009.
nodes.details:
**Atmospheric aerosol loading** appears on both diagrams (slides 6–7). Standard background: **aerosols** are tiny particles suspended in the air – soot, sulphates, dust – from **fossil-fuel and biomass burning**, industry and natural sources. They scatter or absorb sunlight, influence **cloud formation and monsoon rainfall**, and cause respiratory disease (air pollution).

**Status:**
- **2009** (slide 6): "**not yet quantified**".
- **2025** (slide 7): **within the safe operating space** globally (the diagram shows it in green), though regional air pollution can still be severe – e.g. haze from peat and forest fires in Indonesia, and urban emissions in Jakarta/Bandung (W4).

It is one of only **two boundaries still safe**, alongside stratospheric ozone.

nodes.label: Planetary boundaries & doughnut economics
nodes.summary: Raworth's doughnut uses planetary boundaries as its outer ecological ceiling and adds an inner social foundation, defining a safe and just space.
nodes.details:
From the lecturer's notes on slide 7:

- **Doughnut economics** (Kate Raworth) is **built directly on the planetary boundaries framework**.
- Its **outer ring** is the planetary boundaries model repurposed as an **ecological ceiling**, beyond which humanity risks destabilising Earth systems such as **climate, biosphere integrity and biogeochemical flows**.
- Raworth paired this with an **inner ring – the social foundation**, derived loosely from **SDG-type deprivation thresholds** (food, water, health, education, etc.).
- The space between = the **safe and just space** between **ecological overshoot** and **social shortfall**.

**Key contrast:**
- **Planetary boundaries alone** = a **biophysical** model with **no inherent theory of human wellbeing or distribution**.
- **Doughnut economics** uses it as **one half of a normative claim** about what an economy is for – meeting human needs **without breaching** the boundaries.

See the W1 Doughnut Economics diagram.
nodes.examTips: Contrast: planetary boundaries = biophysical (no wellbeing/distribution theory); doughnut = normative (adds social foundation).

nodes.label: Natural capital degradation
nodes.summary: Major human impacts on deserts, grasslands, forests, mountains, marine ecosystems and coral reefs (Miller & Spoolman 2019), e.g. half of coastal wetlands lost.
nodes.details:
Slides 11–12 (Miller & Spoolman, 2019) summarise **natural capital degradation** – how human activities damage ecosystems.

**Terrestrial ecosystems (slide 11):**
- **Deserts** – large desert cities (e.g. Las Vegas), soil/habitat destruction by off-road vehicles, **groundwater depletion**, mining pollution.
- **Grasslands** – conversion to cropland, CO2 release from burning grassland, **overgrazing** by livestock, oil production in arctic tundra.
- **Forests** – clearing for agriculture, grazing, timber and urban development; conversion of diverse forests to **tree plantations**; stream pollution.
- **Mountains** – agriculture, timber and mineral extraction, **hydroelectric dams**, air pollution from cities and power plants.

**Marine ecosystems & coral reefs (slide 12):**
- **Half of coastal wetlands** lost to agriculture and urban development.
- **Over one-fifth of mangrove forests** lost to agriculture, aquaculture and development.
- Beach erosion; ocean-bottom habitat degraded by **dredging and trawling**.
- **At least 20% of coral reefs severely damaged, 25–33% more threatened**.
- Reef stresses: ocean warming, **rising acidity**, sea-level rise, soil erosion, **algae from fertiliser runoff**, **bleaching**, increased UV, anchor/fishing/diving damage.

These impacts are the ground-level picture behind the transgressed boundaries.

nodes.label: Discussion: boundaries, ethics & action
nodes.summary: Questions on a future with more boundaries breached, whether local actions suffice, ethical responsibilities of actors, and balancing development with limits.
nodes.details:
**Questions** (slide 13 and notes):
1. Imagine **two (or three) more boundaries** breached – what would the world and daily life be like?
2. Do **local actions** (less plastic, saving water) help maintain boundaries? **Enough, or do we need global efforts?**
3. What **ethical responsibilities** do individuals, corporations, communities and governments have?
4. How do **planetary boundaries and the tragedy of the commons** intersect? Example?
5. How can **developing countries** balance development with staying within boundaries?

**Model answer outline:**
- *Future*: only ozone and aerosols remain safe; breaching them means more UV (health, crops, reefs) and disrupted monsoons/air quality, compounding food and water insecurity.
- *Local vs global*: local actions reduce pressure and build norms, but boundaries are **global commons** – they need treaties and regulation (Montreal Protocol, Paris Agreement).
- *Ethics*: link to W1 – **stewardship** for individuals, accountability for corporations, regulation by governments, customary rules in communities.
- *Commons link*: the atmosphere as open access → climate change; open-sea overfishing → biosphere loss.
- *Development*: trade-offs; differentiated responsibility of the Global North (W4, W6 CBDR).
nodes.examTips: Essay-ready: connect tragedy of the commons (Part 1) to planetary boundaries (Part 2) with the atmosphere/climate example.

nodes.label: Week 3: Overpopulation vs Overconsumption
nodes.summary: Is environmental damage driven by how many people there are, or by how much and how they consume?
nodes.details:
Week 3 asks whether the planet's limits are threatened mainly by **population** or by **consumption**. It is organised in four parts:

- **3.1 Planetary boundaries & carrying capacity** - carrying capacity, J vs S growth curves, **Malthus** and **Neo-Malthusian** views, overpopulation, technology and the demographic transition, and the **Kerala** case.
- **3.2 Thinking about environmental impact** - the **IPAT** equation (Ehrlich & Holdren), P and A data, the 2050 'factor five' scenario, the **dual role of technology**, the **Jevons paradox**, Kuznets/Kurzweil optimism and **environmental justice** (offshoring, EV batteries, AI data centres).
- **3.3 Over-consumption** - overconsumption, addictive consumption and **hyperconsumption**.
- **3.4 Ecological footprint** - footprint vs **biocapacity**, measurement in global hectares, Indonesia's deficit and 'how many Earths'.

The through-line: **population size alone does not determine impact** - affluence, technology, distribution and governance matter, and the richest consume far more than their share.

nodes.label: Part 3.1: Planetary Limits & Carrying Capacity
nodes.summary: Earth has limits; population growth, technology and development interact with carrying capacity.
nodes.details:
Part 3.1 links last week's **planetary boundaries** to the ecological idea of **carrying capacity** and then to the historical population debate.

- Starts from the 'take-home message' of Rio+20: development must stay within planetary limits.
- **Carrying capacity**: limiting factors cap population growth (S-shaped curve).
- **Malthus** (resources grow linearly, population exponentially -> crisis) and the **Neo-Malthusians** (social, economic and technological drivers of scarcity; Barry Commoner on technology).
- World population data (1 billion in 1804 -> 8 billion in 2022) and the distinction between **population growth** and **overpopulation**.
- Technology (Green Revolution) raises *effective* carrying capacity; GDP-energy-emission data show the link is not proportional.
- **Demographic transition**: falling population may be an *effect* of development rather than its cause, illustrated by **Kerala, India**.

nodes.label: Future We Want & Safe Operating Space
nodes.summary: Since Rio 1992 development must balance economy, society and environment within planetary boundaries; 7 of 9 already breached.
nodes.details:
The opening 'take-home message' frames the week, citing **'The Future We Want' (Rio+20, 2012)** and **'Realizing the Future We Want for All' (2019)**.

- Since the **Rio Earth Summit (1992)** the world has agreed to steer development by the **compass of sustainability**: economic progress in harmony with **social justice** and **environmental preservation** (the three pillars).
- Human activity must stay within the **planetary boundaries**, the **safe operating space** for humanity (Rockstrom et al.).
- Recall from the previous lecture: **7 out of 9 planetary boundaries have been breached**.

Why it matters: carrying capacity, the ecological footprint and overshoot (later in this week) are all ways of asking whether humanity is living within these limits. It connects Week 2 (planetary boundaries) to Week 3's question of *who* and *what* pushes us past them.

nodes.label: Carrying Capacity
nodes.summary: Maximum number of individuals of a species a habitat can sustainably support, set by limiting factors; growth follows an S-curve.
nodes.details:
**Carrying capacity (K)** is the **maximum number of individuals of a species that a particular habitat can sustainably support**.

- It is set by **limiting factors**: **space**, **abiotic** factors (water, nutrients, climate) and **biotic** factors (e.g. **disease**, predators, competition).
- **J-curve (exponential growth)**: happens when resources are effectively unlimited, i.e. early on, when the population is still far below K.
